source: Written 2026-10-17 by Claude Sonnet and solved blind by Claude Opus (Claude Code agents, not runAi: no ai_runs rows), code-checked by lintQuestion; "checked" questions await a platform admin. Hand-written fixture questions are "approved".

notes.NC26.M1.RMM.1: The modeling cycle is tested through text-only models (stating assumptions, predicting, comparing with data, revising, critiquing); no open-ended modeling task can be machine-checked.
notes.NC26.M1.ANFR.2: Predicting from graphs is not testable without a figure; tables are written out as lists of values instead.
notes.NC26.M1.ANFR.3: Graph-based features (growth/decay, domain and range) are tested from equations and written values rather than pictures.
notes.NC26.M1.ANFR.5: Solving by graph or technology is not tested (needs a figure or a tool); the exponential equation question is solved by inspection of powers.
notes.NC26.M1.ANFR.6: Graphing the solution region is not tested (needs a figure); questions use points, boundary lines and interpretation in context.
notes.NC26.M1.ANFR.7: Solving by graphing is tested only through the crossing point of two written lines and the count of solutions; no picture is used.
notes.NC26.M1.SGMR.1: Figures are given by coordinates in the question text; no picture is referred to.
notes.NC26.M1.SGMR.2: Text only: the congruence criteria are tested by described measurements; no figures. Hypotenuse-leg is deliberately left out (not clearly part of the Math 1 summary).
notes.NC26.M1.SGMR.3: All coordinates are written out. Triangle area uses a horizontal base so no shoelace formula is needed.
notes.NC26.M1.SDSR.1: Two-way tables are given as sentences listing every cell. Probabilities may be entered as equivalent fractions or decimals.
notes.NC26.M1.SDSR.2: Mostly conceptual, so mostly choice questions; two numeric ones (response rate, count of statistical questions).
notes.NC26.M1.SDSR.3: Datasets are given as counts in words. The splitting-by-a-third-variable item gives all the numbers so the explanation can be checked.
notes.NC26.M1.SDSR.4: Scatter plots are given as lists of ordered pairs, or described in words; no figures. The misleading-bar-graph item describes the axis in words.
notes.NC26.M1.SDSR.5: No regression is computed by hand (it needs technology); questions use given lines, r values and a described residual plot.
notes.NC26.M1.SDSR.6: Mostly critique of claims, so mostly choice; the numeric ones are percent calculations in context.

questions.skill: Name an assumption built into a model
questions.stem: Maya models the cost of a taxi ride with $C = 3 + 2m$, where $C$ is the cost in dollars and $m$ is the number of miles. Which assumption is built into this model?
choices: Longer rides cost more per mile
Every mile costs the same amount
There is no charge before the ride begins
The cost changes with the time of day
questions.answer: Every mile costs the same amount
questions.solution: In $C = 3 + 2m$ the cost rises by 2 dollars for every extra mile, so each mile costs the same. The 3 is a starting charge, and time of day does not appear in the model.

solve.answer: Every mile costs the same amount
solve.work: C = 3 + 2m: a fixed 3 dollars plus 2 dollars for each mile, so every mile adds the same 2 dollars (constant rate). Time of day is not in the model; cost per mile does not grow; and at m = 0 the cost is 3, so there IS a charge before any miles, making the last option false.

questions.skill: Use a model to make a prediction
questions.stem: A candle is 20 centimeters tall when lit and burns down 2 centimeters each hour. A student models its height with $h = 20 - 2t$, where $h$ is the height in centimeters after $t$ hours. According to the model, how tall is the candle after 6 hours, in centimeters?
questions.solution: Put $t = 6$ into the model: $h = 20 - 2 \times 6 = 20 - 12 = 8$ centimeters.

questions.skill: Revise a model when it disagrees with measurements
questions.stem: A student's model predicts that a plant will be 30 centimeters tall after 4 weeks. After 4 weeks the plant is measured and is 22 centimeters tall. What should the student do next?
choices: Revise the model so it fits the measurement better
Keep the model, because the prediction must be correct
Change the measurement to match the prediction
Decide that plants cannot be modeled
questions.answer: Revise the model so it fits the measurement better
questions.solution: A model is tested against real data. The prediction is 8 centimeters too high, so the student should look for what the model missed and revise it. Changing the measurement or giving up is not how the modeling cycle works.

solve.answer: Revise the model so it fits the measurement better
solve.work: Prediction 30, measurement 22: the model does not fit the data, so in the modeling cycle the student revises the model. Changing data, insisting the model is right, or giving up are all wrong.

questions.skill: Compare a model prediction with observed data
questions.stem: A student models her savings with $S = 40 + 15w$, where $S$ is her savings in dollars after $w$ weeks. After 3 weeks she really has 90 dollars. How many dollars more is her real savings than the model predicts?
questions.solution: The model predicts $S = 40 + 15 \times 3 = 85$ dollars. She really has 90 dollars, which is $90 - 85 = 5$ dollars more.

questions.skill: Critique a model using measured data
questions.stem: A student models a tank that starts with 100 liters and empties at a constant 4 liters per minute: $V = 100 - 4t$. Measurements show 60 liters after 10 minutes and 35 liters after 20 minutes. Which statement is the best critique of the model?
choices: The tank empties faster over time, so the rate should be larger
The model matches at 10 minutes, so it is right at every time
The model is wrong because the tank cannot start with 100 liters
The tank empties more slowly over time, so a constant rate is a poor assumption
questions.answer: The tank empties more slowly over time, so a constant rate is a poor assumption
questions.solution: At 10 minutes the model gives $100 - 40 = 60$ liters, which matches. At 20 minutes it gives $100 - 80 = 20$ liters, but 35 liters were measured. The tank has more water left than predicted, so it empties more slowly as time goes on. Matching at one time does not make a model right everywhere.

solve.answer: The tank empties more slowly over time, so a constant rate is a poor assumption
solve.work: Model: V(10) = 60 (matches), V(20) = 20 but measured 35. Data: lost 40 L in first 10 min (4 L/min), 25 L in next 10 min (2.5 L/min), so draining slows; constant rate is a poor assumption. Option 1 overgeneralizes, option 3 is unsupported, option 4 has the direction wrong.

questions.skill: Use a model to answer a question within a limit
questions.stem: Printing $n$ flyers costs $C = 12 + 0.25n$ dollars. A club has 62 dollars to spend. What is the greatest number of flyers the club can print?
questions.solution: The club can spend at most 62 dollars: $12 + 0.25n \le 62$, so $0.25n \le 50$ and $n \le 200$. The greatest number is 200 flyers.

questions.skill: Choose the model that fits recorded data
questions.stem: A scientist counts bacteria each hour and records 800, 1200, 1800 and 2700 at hours 0, 1, 2 and 3. Which model fits all of these counts?
questions.solution: Each count is 1.5 times the one before: $800 \times 1.5 = 1200$, $1200 \times 1.5 = 1800$, $1800 \times 1.5 = 2700$. So $N = 800(1.5)^t$. The linear model $800 + 400t$ matches only the first two counts (it gives 1600 at hour 2).

questions.skill: Test a model against a dealer value and find the error
questions.stem: A student models the value of a car with $V = 20{,}000(0.8)^t$ dollars after $t$ years, assuming it loses 20% of its value each year. A dealer says the car is worth $10{,}500$ dollars after 3 years. How many dollars more is the dealer's value than the model predicts?
questions.solution: The model predicts $V = 20{,}000(0.8)^3 = 20{,}000 \times 0.512 = 10{,}240$ dollars. The dealer says $10{,}500$, which is $10{,}500 - 10{,}240 = 260$ dollars more.

questions.skill: Judge the limits of a model
questions.stem: A student models the height of a young tree with $h = 2 + 3t$ meters after $t$ years, and uses it to predict a height of 152 meters after 50 years. Which is the best critique of this prediction?
choices: The model assumes steady growth, but trees slow down as they get very tall
The model is invalid because the tree starts above zero height
The prediction is reliable because the formula was worked out correctly
The model is invalid because time is measured in years
questions.answer: The model assumes steady growth, but trees slow down as they get very tall
questions.solution: The model adds 3 meters every year without end, which gives an unrealistic 152 meters. A good critique looks at whether the assumption (constant growth) still makes sense far from the data. The starting height and the unit of time are not problems.

solve.answer: The model assumes steady growth, but trees slow down as they get very tall
solve.work: h(50) = 2 + 150 = 152 m, arithmetically right but unrealistic: a linear model assumes the tree keeps growing 3 m a year forever, while real trees slow down. Units in years and a nonzero start are not flaws; correct arithmetic does not make the extrapolation reliable.

questions.skill: Multiply powers with the same base
questions.stem: Simplify $x^3 \cdot x^4$.
questions.solution: When you multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents: $x^3 \cdot x^4 = x^{3+4} = x^7$.

solve.work: Same base, add exponents: x^(3+4) = x^7.

questions.skill: Evaluate zero and positive integer exponents
questions.stem: What is the value of $5^0 + 3^2$?
questions.solution: Any nonzero number to the power 0 is 1, so $5^0 = 1$. Also $3^2 = 9$. The sum is $1 + 9 = 10$.

questions.skill: Add polynomials by combining like terms
questions.stem: Add $(4x^2 + 3x + 1) + (x^2 + 6x + 5)$. What is the coefficient of $x$ in the sum?
questions.solution: Combine like terms: $(4x^2 + x^2) + (3x + 6x) + (1 + 5) = 5x^2 + 9x + 6$. The coefficient of $x$ is 9.

solve.work: Sum = 5x^2 + 9x + 6. Coefficient of x is 3 + 6 = 9.

questions.skill: Subtract polynomials, distributing the negative
questions.solution: Subtracting changes the sign of every term in the second polynomial: $5x^2 + 3x - 4 - 2x^2 + x - 6$. Combine like terms: $3x^2 + 4x - 10$.

questions.skill: Multiply two binomials
questions.stem: Multiply: $(x + 4)(x - 2)$.
questions.solution: Multiply each term by each term: $x \cdot x + x(-2) + 4 \cdot x + 4(-2) = x^2 - 2x + 4x - 8 = x^2 + 2x - 8$.

questions.skill: Use an area model for a product
questions.stem: A rectangle has width $x + 2$ and length $x + 6$. Cutting it into four smaller rectangles gives areas $x^2$, $6x$, $2x$ and 12. The total area is $x^2 + bx + c$. What is $b$?
questions.solution: The four parts add to $x^2 + 6x + 2x + 12 = x^2 + 8x + 12$. So $b = 8$.

solve.work: (x + 2)(x + 6) = x^2 + 6x + 2x + 12 = x^2 + 8x + 12, matching the four pieces. b = 8.

questions.skill: Divide powers with negative exponents
questions.stem: Simplify $\frac{x^5 y^{-2}}{x^2 y^{-6}}$, where $x$ and $y$ are not zero.
questions.solution: When you divide powers with the same base, subtract the exponents. For $x$: $5 - 2 = 3$. For $y$: $-2 - (-6) = -2 + 6 = 4$. The result is $x^3 y^4$.

questions.skill: Find a coefficient after multiplying binomials
questions.stem: When $(2x - 1)(x + 4)$ is written in the form $ax^2 + bx + c$, what is $b$?
questions.solution: $(2x - 1)(x + 4) = 2x^2 + 8x - x - 4 = 2x^2 + 7x - 4$. The middle terms $8x$ and $-x$ combine to $7x$, so $b = 7$.

questions.skill: Raise a product to a power
questions.stem: Simplify $(3x^2 y)^3$.
questions.solution: Cube every factor: $3^3 = 27$, $(x^2)^3 = x^6$ (multiply exponents) and $y^3$. The result is $27x^6y^3$.

questions.skill: Recognize an arithmetic sequence
questions.stem: Which list of numbers is an arithmetic sequence?
questions.solution: An arithmetic sequence adds the same number each time. 5, 9, 13, 17 adds 4 every time. 2, 6, 18, 54 and 3, 6, 12, 24 multiply by the same number, and 1, 2, 4, 7 adds 1, then 2, then 3.

solve.work: 5,9,13,17: differences 4,4,4 -> arithmetic. 1,2,4,7: differences 1,2,3 no. 3,6,12,24 and 2,6,18,54 are geometric with non-constant differences.

questions.skill: Continue a geometric pattern
questions.stem: A pattern begins 4, 12, 36, 108. Each number is the same multiple of the number before it. What is the next number in the pattern?
questions.solution: Each number is 3 times the one before it: $4 \times 3 = 12$, $12 \times 3 = 36$, $36 \times 3 = 108$. The next is $108 \times 3 = 324$.

questions.skill: Match a situation to exponential growth
questions.stem: Which situation is best described by exponential growth?
choices: A plumber charges 40 dollars plus 15 dollars per hour
The number of views of a video doubles every day
A runner covers 3 kilometers every 15 minutes
A tree grows 4 centimeters every year
questions.answer: The number of views of a video doubles every day
questions.solution: Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each step. Doubling every day is multiplying by 2. The other three situations add the same amount each time, so they are linear.

solve.answer: The number of views of a video doubles every day
solve.work: Doubling every day is a constant multiplier -> exponential. The other three add a constant amount per unit -> linear.

questions.skill: Tell linear from exponential in a table
questions.stem: A table gives $y$ for $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$: the values of $y$ are 3, 6, 12, 24. Which statement describes the pattern?
choices: Exponential: $y$ is multiplied by 2 each time $x$ increases by 1
Linear: $y$ increases by 3 each time $x$ increases by 1
Linear: $y$ increases by 6 each time $x$ increases by 1
Exponential: $y$ is multiplied by 3 each time $x$ increases by 1
questions.answer: Exponential: $y$ is multiplied by 2 each time $x$ increases by 1
questions.solution: The differences are 3, 6, 12, which are not equal, so the pattern is not linear. The ratios are $6 \div 3 = 2$, $12 \div 6 = 2$ and $24 \div 12 = 2$, so $y$ is multiplied by 2 each time.

solve.answer: Exponential: $y$ is multiplied by 2 each time $x$ increases by 1
solve.work: 3,6,12,24: differences 3,6,12 not constant; ratios 2,2,2 -> exponential, multiplied by 2.

questions.skill: Predict a value in an exponential decay pattern
questions.stem: A table gives $P$ for $t = 0, 1, 2, 3$: the values of $P$ are 640, 320, 160, 80. The pattern continues in the same way. What is $P$ when $t = 6$?
questions.solution: Each value is half the one before it. So $P = 640 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^t$. At $t = 6$: $640 \div 64 = 10$. (Continuing the list: 80, 40, 20, 10.)

questions.skill: Predict a value in a linear pattern from a table
questions.stem: A table gives $y$ for $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$: the values of $y$ are 10, 14, 18, 22. The pattern continues in the same way. What is $y$ when $x = 6$?
questions.solution: The values go up by 4 each time, so $y = 10 + 4x$. When $x = 6$: $y = 10 + 24 = 34$.

solve.work: Adds 4 each step: y = 10 + 4x. At x = 6: 10 + 24 = 34.

questions.skill: Recognize a table that is neither linear nor exponential
questions.stem: Four tables each give $y$ for $x = 1, 2, 3, 4$. Which table is neither linear nor exponential?
questions.solution: For 2, 5, 10, 17 the differences are 3, 5, 7 (not equal) and the ratios are 2.5, 2, 1.7 (not equal), so it is neither. 2, 5, 8, 11 adds 3 each time, 2, 6, 18, 54 multiplies by 3, and 32, 16, 8, 4 multiplies by one half.

solve.work: 32,16,8,4: ratio 1/2 exponential. 2,5,10,17: differences 3,5,7 (not constant), ratios 2.5, 2, 1.7 (not constant) -> neither (quadratic, x^2+1). 2,6,18,54: ratio 3 exponential. 2,5,8,11: difference 3 linear.

questions.skill: Compare a linear and an exponential plan
questions.stem: Plan A has value $A = 100 + 20t$ and Plan B has value $B = 20(2)^t$ after $t$ whole years. For the first whole number of years $t$ where Plan B is greater than Plan A, what is $t$?
questions.solution: Compare year by year. $t = 0$: A is 100, B is 20. $t = 1$: 120 and 40. $t = 2$: 140 and 80. $t = 3$: 160 and 160, which are equal, not greater. $t = 4$: A is 180 and B is 320, so Plan B is greater for the first time at $t = 4$.

solve.work: t=0: A 100, B 20. t=1: 120 vs 40. t=2: 140 vs 80. t=3: 160 vs 160 (equal, not greater). t=4: 180 vs 320 -> B greater. t = 4.

questions.skill: Find a later term of an arithmetic sequence from two terms
questions.stem: In an arithmetic sequence, the 3rd term is 11 and the 7th term is 31. What is the 10th term?
questions.solution: From the 3rd to the 7th term there are 4 steps, and the terms rise by $31 - 11 = 20$, so each step adds $20 \div 4 = 5$. The 10th term is 3 steps after the 7th: $31 + 3 \times 5 = 46$.

questions.skill: Evaluate a function written with function notation
questions.stem: If $f(x) = 3x - 2$, what is $f(4)$?

questions.skill: Choose a reasonable domain in context
questions.stem: A bakery sells muffins for 2 dollars each, so the cost of $n$ muffins is $C(n) = 2n$ dollars. Which set is the most reasonable domain of $C$?
choices: All real numbers
The even numbers 0, 2, 4, 6, and so on
All real numbers greater than 2
Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on
questions.answer: Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on
questions.solution: The domain is the set of possible inputs. You cannot buy part of a muffin or a negative number of muffins, so the inputs are the whole numbers. The even numbers 0, 2, 4, 6 are the possible costs (outputs), not the inputs.

solve.answer: Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, and so on
solve.work: You buy a whole number of muffins, including possibly 0: domain {0,1,2,...}. Not all reals, not only evens, not reals > 2.

questions.skill: Tell growth from decay
questions.stem: Which statement describes $f(x) = 5(0.8)^x$?
choices: Exponential decay
Exponential growth
Linear increase
Linear decrease
questions.answer: Exponential decay
questions.solution: The variable is in the exponent, so the function is exponential. The base 0.8 is less than 1, so each step multiplies the value by 0.8 and it gets smaller: decay.

solve.answer: Exponential decay
solve.work: Form a(b)^x with a = 5 > 0 and 0 < b = 0.8 < 1 -> exponential decay.

questions.skill: Evaluate a function in context
questions.stem: A plant's height after $w$ weeks is $h(w) = 4 + 2.5w$ centimeters. What is $h(6)$, in centimeters?

questions.skill: Find an average rate of change
questions.stem: For a function $f$, $f(2) = 7$ and $f(6) = 19$. What is the average rate of change of $f$ from $x = 2$ to $x = 6$?
questions.solution: Average rate of change is the change in output divided by the change in input: $\frac{19 - 7}{6 - 2} = \frac{12}{4} = 3$.

questions.skill: Decide whether a function in context is discrete or continuous
questions.stem: A car travels at a steady 60 miles per hour, so after $t$ hours it has gone $d(t) = 60t$ miles, where $t$ can be any time from 0 to 5 hours. Which statement is true?
choices: The graph is discrete because distance is measured in miles
The graph is continuous because $t$ can be any value from 0 to 5
The graph is discrete because 60 is a whole number
The graph is continuous only because it passes through the origin
questions.answer: The graph is continuous because $t$ can be any value from 0 to 5
questions.solution: A function is continuous when its inputs can be any value in an interval. Time can be any value from 0 to 5 hours, including parts of an hour, so the graph is continuous. The units and the number 60 do not decide this.

solve.answer: The graph is continuous because $t$ can be any value from 0 to 5
solve.work: Time can take any value in [0, 5], so the graph is an unbroken segment: continuous for that reason. The other options give wrong reasons.

questions.skill: Find the range of an exponential function
questions.stem: Let $g(x) = 2(3)^x$ for all real numbers $x$. What is the range of $g$?
choices: All real numbers
$y \ge 2$
$y \ge 0$
questions.solution: A positive number raised to any power is positive, and $2(3)^x$ gets as close to 0 as you like for very negative $x$ without ever reaching it. So every output is greater than 0, and every positive number is an output: $y > 0$.

solve.work: 3^x > 0 for all real x and takes every positive value, so 2(3)^x takes every value > 0, never 0. Range y > 0. (y >= 2 is wrong: e.g. g(-1) = 2/3.)

questions.skill: Compare the rates of change of two functions
questions.stem: Function $f$ is $f(x) = 5x - 2$. Function $g$ is linear with $g(0) = 1$, $g(2) = 9$ and $g(4) = 17$. Which function has the greater rate of change, and what are the two rates?
choices: $g$ has the greater rate: 8 compared with 5
$g$ has the greater rate: 16 compared with 5
$f$ has the greater rate: 5 compared with 4
The rates are equal: both are 4
questions.answer: $f$ has the greater rate: 5 compared with 4
questions.solution: The rate of change of $f$ is its slope, 5. For $g$, the output rises from 1 to 9 while the input rises by 2, so the rate is $\frac{9 - 1}{2} = 4$ (the same from 2 to 4: $\frac{17 - 9}{2} = 4$). Since $5 > 4$, $f$ has the greater rate.

solve.answer: $f$ has the greater rate: 5 compared with 4

questions.skill: Average rate of change of an exponential function
questions.stem: Let $f(x) = 3(2)^x$. What is the average rate of change of $f$ from $x = 1$ to $x = 3$?
questions.solution: $f(1) = 3(2) = 6$ and $f(3) = 3(8) = 24$. The average rate of change is $\frac{24 - 6}{3 - 1} = \frac{18}{2} = 9$.

questions.skill: Write a linear function from a situation
questions.stem: A gym charges 25 dollars to join and then 10 dollars per month. Which function gives the total cost $f(m)$ in dollars after $m$ months?
questions.solution: The joining fee is paid once (25), and 10 dollars is added for each month, so $f(m) = 25 + 10m$.

solve.work: One-time 25 plus 10 per month: f(m) = 25 + 10m.

questions.skill: Use a recursive rule for an arithmetic sequence
questions.stem: A sequence has $a_1 = 6$ and $a_n = a_{n-1} + 4$ for $n \ge 2$. What is $a_4$?
questions.solution: Start with 6 and add 4 each time: $a_1 = 6$, $a_2 = 10$, $a_3 = 14$, $a_4 = 18$.

questions.skill: Write slope-intercept form from slope and intercept
questions.stem: A line has slope 2 and crosses the y-axis at the point $(0, -3)$. Which equation is the equation of the line?
questions.solution: Slope-intercept form is $y = mx + b$, with slope $m = 2$ and y-intercept $b = -3$. So $y = 2x - 3$.

solve.work: y = mx + b with m = 2, b = -3: y = 2x - 3.

questions.skill: Write an exponential function from a situation
questions.stem: A deposit of 300 dollars grows by 5% each year. Which function gives the balance $B(t)$ in dollars after $t$ years?
questions.solution: Growing by 5% each year means multiplying by $1 + 0.05 = 1.05$ each year, so $B(t) = 300(1.05)^t$.

solve.work: Growth of 5% per year multiplies by 1.05 each year: B(t) = 300(1.05)^t.

questions.skill: Find the y-intercept of a line through two points
questions.stem: A line passes through the points $(1, 5)$ and $(3, 11)$. What is its y-intercept?
questions.solution: The slope is $\frac{11 - 5}{3 - 1} = 3$. Using $y = 3x + b$ and the point $(1, 5)$: $5 = 3 + b$, so $b = 2$.

questions.skill: Use a recursive rule for a geometric sequence
questions.stem: A sequence has $f(1) = 2$ and $f(n) = 3 \cdot f(n-1)$ for $n \ge 2$. What is $f(5)$?

questions.skill: Choose the function that models a table of values
questions.stem: A table gives $y$ for $x = 0, 1, 2, 3$: the values of $y$ are 5, 15, 45, 135. Which function fits all four values?
questions.solution: Each value is 3 times the one before, and $y = 5$ when $x = 0$, so $y = 5(3)^x$. The linear rule $5 + 10x$ gives 25 at $x = 2$, not 45. $15(3)^x$ gives 15 at $x = 0$.

solve.work: Start 5 at x = 0, ratio 3: y = 5(3)^x gives 5, 15, 45, 135. 5 + 10x gives 25 at x = 2; 15(3)^x gives 15 at x = 0; 3(5)^x gives 3 at x = 0.

questions.skill: Evaluate a two-step recursive rule
questions.stem: A sequence has $a_1 = 3$ and $a_n = 2a_{n-1} - 1$ for $n \ge 2$. What is $a_5$?

questions.skill: Write a linear model from two measurements
questions.stem: A candle burns down at a constant rate. After 2 hours it is 30 centimeters tall, and after 5 hours it is 24 centimeters tall. How tall, in centimeters, was it when it was first lit (at time 0)?
questions.solution: In 3 hours the height fell by 6 centimeters, so the candle burns down 2 centimeters per hour. Going back 2 hours from the first measurement adds $2 \times 2 = 4$ centimeters: $30 + 4 = 34$ centimeters.

questions.skill: Solve a one-step-plus-one linear equation
questions.stem: Solve for $x$: $3x + 5 = 20$.
questions.solution: Subtract 5 from both sides: $3x = 15$. Divide both sides by 3: $x = 5$.

questions.skill: Solve a formula for one quantity
questions.stem: The formula $d = rt$ relates distance $d$, rate $r$ and time $t$. Solve the formula for $t$.
choices: $t = dr$
$t = \frac{r}{d}$
$t = \frac{d}{r}$
$t = d - r$
questions.answer: $t = \frac{d}{r}$
questions.solution: To get $t$ alone, divide both sides of $d = rt$ by $r$: $t = \frac{d}{r}$.

solve.answer: $t = \frac{d}{r}$
solve.work: Divide both sides of d = rt by r: t = d/r.

questions.skill: Justify a step in solving an equation
questions.stem: In solving $4x - 7 = 21$, a student writes the next line as $4x = 28$. Which property justifies this step?
choices: Addition property of equality
Multiplication property of equality
Distributive property
Commutative property of addition
questions.answer: Addition property of equality
questions.solution: The student added 7 to both sides: $4x - 7 + 7 = 21 + 7$. Adding the same number to both sides of an equation keeps it true, which is the addition property of equality.

solve.answer: Addition property of equality
solve.work: From 4x - 7 = 21 to 4x = 28, 7 is added to both sides: addition property of equality.

questions.skill: Solve a linear inequality, reversing the sign
questions.stem: Solve the inequality $-2x + 3 < 11$.
questions.solution: Subtract 3 from both sides: $-2x < 8$. Dividing both sides by $-2$ reverses the inequality sign: $x > -4$.

solve.work: -2x + 3 < 11 -> -2x < 8 -> divide by -2 and flip: x > -4. Check x = 0: 3 < 11 true.

questions.skill: Solve a formula for a quantity, given a value
questions.stem: The formula $F = \frac{9}{5}C + 32$ changes a temperature in degrees Celsius $C$ to degrees Fahrenheit $F$. A temperature is 68 degrees Fahrenheit. What is it in degrees Celsius?
questions.solution: Put $F = 68$ in the formula: $68 = \frac{9}{5}C + 32$. Subtract 32: $36 = \frac{9}{5}C$. Multiply by $\frac{5}{9}$: $C = 36 \times \frac{5}{9} = 20$.

questions.skill: Solve a simple exponential equation in context
questions.stem: A culture starts with 3 bacteria and triples every hour, so after $t$ hours it has $3 \cdot 3^t$ bacteria. After how many hours are there 243 bacteria?
questions.solution: Solve $3 \cdot 3^t = 243$. Divide by 3: $3^t = 81$. Since $3^4 = 81$, $t = 4$ hours. (Check: 3, 9, 27, 81, 243.)

questions.skill: Write an exponential equation from a situation
questions.stem: A population starts at 200 and doubles every hour. Which equation can be solved to find the number of hours $t$ until the population is 3200?
questions.solution: The starting amount is 200 and it is multiplied by 2 for each hour, so after $t$ hours the population is $200(2)^t$. Setting that equal to 3200 gives $200(2)^t = 3200$.

solve.work: Population after t hours = 200(2)^t; set equal to 3200: 200(2)^t = 3200 (t = 4).

questions.skill: Interpret the solution of an inequality in context
questions.stem: You have 52 dollars. Park entry costs 14 dollars, and each ride ticket costs 3 dollars. You can only buy whole tickets. What is the greatest number of ride tickets you can buy?
questions.solution: The inequality is $14 + 3r \le 52$, so $3r \le 38$ and $r \le 12.67\ldots$. You can only buy whole tickets, so the greatest number is 12 (12 tickets cost 36 dollars, for a total of 50 dollars).

questions.skill: Solve a formula for time, given values
questions.stem: The formula $A = P + Prt$ gives the total $A$ in dollars after $t$ years when $P$ dollars earn simple interest at yearly rate $r$ (written as a decimal). When $P = 200$ and $r = 0.05$, the total is $A = 230$. How many years is that?
questions.solution: Put in the values: $230 = 200 + 200(0.05)t = 200 + 10t$. Subtract 200: $30 = 10t$. So $t = 3$ years.

questions.skill: Test a point in a two-variable inequality
questions.stem: Which point is a solution of $y \ge x + 1$?
questions.solution: Put each point in. For $(1, 3)$: $3 \ge 1 + 1 = 2$ is true. For $(3, 1)$: $1 \ge 4$ is false. For $(2, 2)$: $2 \ge 3$ is false. For $(4, 4)$: $4 \ge 5$ is false.

questions.skill: Find the boundary value of y for a given x
questions.stem: The inequality is $y < 3x + 2$. For the point $(4, y)$ to be a solution, what is the greatest whole number that $y$ can be?
questions.solution: When $x = 4$: $y < 3(4) + 2 = 14$. The greatest whole number less than 14 is 13.

solve.work: y < 3(4) + 2 = 14 (strict). Greatest whole number y = 13.

questions.skill: Write a linear inequality from a context
questions.stem: A theater sells child tickets for 5 dollars each ($x$ of them) and adult tickets for 8 dollars each ($y$ of them). Total ticket sales for one show must be at most 200 dollars. Which inequality models this?
questions.solution: Child sales are $5x$ dollars and adult sales are $8y$ dollars, so the total is $5x + 8y$. "At most 200" means $\le 200$.

solve.issues: Minor realism: a theater capping its sales at 'at most' 200 dollars is an odd context (a cost or budget limit reads more naturally), though the maths and key are unambiguous.
solve.work: Child sales 5x, adult sales 8y, total at most 200: 5x + 8y <= 200.

questions.skill: Write an inequality from its boundary line
questions.stem: The solutions of an inequality are all the points above the line $y = 2x - 1$, and points on the line are not solutions. Which inequality is it?
choices: $y \ge 2x - 1$
questions.solution: Points above the line have $y$ greater than $2x - 1$, so the sign is $>$. Points on the line are not included, so it is $>$ and not $\ge$.

solve.work: Above the line, line excluded: strict >, same line y = 2x - 1: y > 2x - 1.

questions.skill: Interpret a solution of an inequality in context
questions.stem: A school buys $x$ notebooks at 3 dollars each and $y$ pens at 2 dollars each. Its budget is 60 dollars, so $3x + 2y \le 60$. If the school buys 12 notebooks, what is the greatest number of pens it can buy?
questions.solution: With $x = 12$: $36 + 2y \le 60$, so $2y \le 24$ and $y \le 12$. The greatest number of pens is 12.

questions.skill: Find a point that is not a solution
questions.stem: Which point is NOT a solution of $2x + 3y \le 12$?

questions.skill: Count whole-number solutions of an inequality
questions.stem: How many ordered pairs $(x, y)$ of positive whole numbers make $x + y \le 5$ true?
questions.solution: List by $x$. If $x = 1$, then $y$ can be 1, 2, 3 or 4 (4 pairs). If $x = 2$: $y$ is 1, 2 or 3 (3 pairs). If $x = 3$: 2 pairs. If $x = 4$: 1 pair. If $x = 5$ there is no positive $y$. Total: $4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10$.

questions.skill: Interpret a solution point in context
questions.stem: A club sells $a$ adult tickets at 15 dollars each and $b$ child tickets at 10 dollars each. To reach its goal, it needs $15a + 10b \ge 120$. What does the solution $(a, b) = (4, 6)$ mean?
choices: Selling 4 adult and 6 child tickets raises more than 120 dollars, so the goal is beaten
Selling 4 adult and 6 child tickets raises exactly 120 dollars, so the goal is just met
Selling 4 adult and 6 child tickets raises less than 120 dollars, so the goal is missed
Selling 4 adult and 6 child tickets raises 4 + 6 = 10 dollars, far below the goal
questions.answer: Selling 4 adult and 6 child tickets raises exactly 120 dollars, so the goal is just met
questions.solution: Put in the numbers: $15(4) + 10(6) = 60 + 60 = 120$, and $120 \ge 120$ is true. The ticket sales raise exactly the 120 dollars needed, so this point lies on the boundary.

solve.answer: Selling 4 adult and 6 child tickets raises exactly 120 dollars, so the goal is just met
solve.work: 15(4) + 10(6) = 60 + 60 = 120, which equals 120, so the goal is exactly met (>= holds with equality).

questions.skill: Use the boundary line of an inequality
questions.stem: The boundary line of the inequality $3x - 2y \ge 6$ is the line $3x - 2y = 6$. The point $(4, k)$ lies on this line. What is $k$?

questions.skill: Solve a system by substitution
questions.stem: A system has the equations $y = 2x$ and $x + y = 12$. What is $x$?
questions.solution: Substitute $y = 2x$ into $x + y = 12$: $x + 2x = 12$, so $3x = 12$ and $x = 4$.

questions.skill: Identify the solution of a system
questions.stem: Which ordered pair is the solution of both $x + y = 7$ and $x - y = 3$?
questions.solution: Check each pair in both equations. For $(5, 2)$: $5 + 2 = 7$ and $5 - 2 = 3$, so it works. $(2, 5)$, $(4, 3)$ and $(3, 4)$ all add to 7 but give $x - y$ equal to $-3$, 1 and $-1$.

questions.skill: Build a system from a situation
questions.stem: A bakery sold 100 items in one day. Muffins ($x$ of them) cost 3 dollars each and bagels ($y$ of them) cost 2 dollars each, and the bakery took in 260 dollars. Which system models this?
questions.solution: The number of items is $x + y = 100$. The money taken in is 3 dollars per muffin plus 2 dollars per bagel: $3x + 2y = 260$.

solve.work: Count: x + y = 100. Money: 3x + 2y = 260 (solution x = 60, y = 40).

questions.skill: Count the solutions of a system
questions.stem: How many solutions does the system $y = 2x + 3$ and $y = 2x - 5$ have?
choices: Exactly one solution
Infinitely many solutions
Exactly two solutions
No solution
questions.answer: No solution
questions.solution: Both lines have slope 2 but different y-intercepts (3 and $-5$), so they are parallel and never meet. Setting the right sides equal gives $2x + 3 = 2x - 5$, which is never true.

solve.answer: No solution
solve.work: Same slope 2, different intercepts 3 and -5: parallel lines, never meet. No solution.

questions.skill: Solve a system from a situation
questions.stem: A rental shop has bikes (2 wheels each) and trikes (3 wheels each). There are 14 vehicles with 38 wheels in all. How many trikes are there?
questions.solution: Let $b$ be bikes and $t$ be trikes. Then $b + t = 14$ and $2b + 3t = 38$. Replacing $b$ with $14 - t$: $2(14 - t) + 3t = 38$, so $28 + t = 38$ and $t = 10$.

questions.skill: Find the intersection of two lines
questions.stem: The lines $y = x + 2$ and $y = -x + 8$ cross at one point. What is the y-coordinate of that point?
questions.solution: At the crossing point the y-values are equal: $x + 2 = -x + 8$, so $2x = 6$ and $x = 3$. Then $y = 3 + 2 = 5$.

questions.skill: Interpret the solution of a system in context
questions.stem: A gym offers Plan A, which costs $y = 30 + 4x$ dollars for $x$ visits, and Plan B, which costs $y = 10 + 6x$ dollars for $x$ visits. The solution of the system is $(10, 70)$. What does it mean?
choices: Plan A costs 10 dollars and Plan B costs 70 dollars
After 10 visits both plans cost the same total, 70 dollars
After 70 visits both plans cost the same total, 10 dollars
Plan B is cheaper no matter how many visits
questions.answer: After 10 visits both plans cost the same total, 70 dollars
questions.solution: The solution is the $(x, y)$ that makes both equations true: at $x = 10$ visits, Plan A costs $30 + 40 = 70$ and Plan B costs $10 + 60 = 70$. So after 10 visits the two plans cost the same, 70 dollars.

solve.answer: After 10 visits both plans cost the same total, 70 dollars
solve.work: x = 10 visits, y = 70 dollars: 30 + 40 = 70 and 10 + 60 = 70. Both plans cost 70 after 10 visits.

questions.skill: Find the value that gives infinitely many solutions
questions.stem: The system $y = 3x + 4$ and $2y = 6x + k$ has infinitely many solutions. What is $k$?
questions.solution: The system has infinitely many solutions when both equations describe the same line. Multiplying $y = 3x + 4$ by 2 gives $2y = 6x + 8$, so $k = 8$.

solve.work: Double the first: 2y = 6x + 8. Same line iff k = 8.

questions.skill: Solve a system by substitution with a coefficient
questions.stem: A system has the equations $3x + 2y = 16$ and $y = x + 3$. What is $y$?

questions.skill: Find the image of a point under a translation
questions.stem: The point $(3, 5)$ is translated 4 units to the right and 2 units down. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.solution: Moving right adds to the x-coordinate: $3 + 4 = 7$. Moving down subtracts from the y-coordinate: $5 - 2 = 3$. The image is $(7, 3)$.

questions.skill: Know what rigid transformations preserve
questions.stem: Which pair of properties is the same for a figure and its image under any rotation, reflection or translation?
choices: Side lengths and angle measures
Side lengths and orientation
Angle measures and location
Location and orientation
questions.answer: Side lengths and angle measures
questions.solution: Rigid transformations keep the shape and size: side lengths and angle measures do not change. A translation, rotation or reflection moves the figure, so its location changes, and a reflection reverses its orientation.

solve.answer: Side lengths and angle measures
solve.work: Rigid motions preserve distance and angle measure. Location changes under translations; orientation is reversed by reflections.

questions.skill: Find the image of a point under a reflection
questions.stem: The point $(-4, 7)$ is reflected across the y-axis. What is the x-coordinate of its image?
questions.solution: A reflection across the y-axis changes the sign of the x-coordinate and keeps the y-coordinate. The image of $(-4, 7)$ is $(4, 7)$, so the x-coordinate is 4.

solve.work: Reflection across y-axis: (x, y) -> (-x, y). (-4, 7) -> (4, 7). x-coordinate 4.

questions.skill: Find the image of a point under a rotation
questions.stem: The point $(2, 5)$ is rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.solution: A 90 degree counterclockwise rotation about the origin takes $(x, y)$ to $(-y, x)$. So $(2, 5)$ becomes $(-5, 2)$.

solve.work: 90 deg CCW about origin: (x, y) -> (-y, x). (2, 5) -> (-5, 2).

questions.skill: Find a preimage using function notation
questions.stem: A translation is given by $T(x, y) = (x - 3, y + 5)$. The image of a point $P$ is $T(P) = (2, 1)$. What is the sum of the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate of $P$?
questions.solution: Undo the translation. The image has $x - 3 = 2$, so $x = 5$, and $y + 5 = 1$, so $y = -4$. So $P = (5, -4)$ and the sum is $5 + (-4) = 1$.

questions.skill: Identify the transformation that maps points to images
questions.stem: A single rigid transformation takes $(2, 3)$ to $(2, -3)$ and $(5, 1)$ to $(5, -1)$. Which transformation is it?
choices: A reflection across the y-axis
A rotation of 180 degrees about the origin
A translation 6 units down
A reflection across the x-axis
questions.answer: A reflection across the x-axis
questions.solution: Each x-coordinate stays the same and each y-coordinate changes sign, which is a reflection across the x-axis. A rotation of 180 degrees would give $(-2, -3)$, a reflection across the y-axis would give $(-2, 3)$, and moving 6 units down would give $(5, -5)$ for the second point.

solve.answer: A reflection across the x-axis
solve.work: (x, y) -> (x, -y) fits both points: reflection across the x-axis. Translation 6 down sends (5,1) to (5,-5); 180 deg rotation sends (2,3) to (-2,-3); y-axis reflection changes x.

questions.skill: Use congruence to find a perimeter after two moves
questions.stem: Triangle ABC has vertices $A(0, 0)$, $B(4, 0)$ and $C(0, 3)$, so $AB = 4$, $AC = 3$ and $BC = 5$. The triangle is reflected across the x-axis and then translated 6 units to the right. What is the perimeter of the final image?
questions.solution: Reflections and translations are rigid transformations, so side lengths do not change. The image is congruent to ABC and has perimeter $4 + 3 + 5 = 12$.

solve.work: Rigid motions preserve lengths, so the image is congruent: perimeter 4 + 3 + 5 = 12.

questions.skill: Undo a sequence of transformations to find the preimage
questions.stem: A figure is translated 5 units to the left and then reflected across the x-axis. The image of one of its points is $(-1, -6)$. What is the sum of the x-coordinate and the y-coordinate of the original point?
questions.solution: Work backwards. Undo the reflection across the x-axis: $(-1, -6)$ becomes $(-1, 6)$. Undo the translation 5 units left by moving 5 units right: $(4, 6)$. The sum is $4 + 6 = 10$. (Check forward: $(4, 6)$ moves left to $(-1, 6)$, then reflects to $(-1, -6)$.)

solve.work: Undo reflection across x-axis: (-1, -6) -> (-1, 6). Undo translation 5 left (move 5 right): (4, 6). Check: (4,6) -> (-1,6) -> (-1,-6). Sum 10.

questions.skill: Describe a sequence of moves that shows congruence
questions.stem: Triangle $T$ has vertices $(0, 0)$, $(2, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$. Triangle $T'$ has vertices $(3, 3)$, $(3, 5)$ and $(2, 3)$. Which sequence of rigid transformations maps $T$ onto $T'$?
choices: Rotate 90 degrees clockwise about the origin, then translate 3 units right and 3 units up
Reflect across the y-axis, then translate 3 units right and 3 units up
Rotate 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 3 units right and 3 units up
Reflect across the x-axis, then translate 3 units right and 3 units up
questions.answer: Rotate 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 3 units right and 3 units up
questions.solution: Rotating 90 degrees counterclockwise takes $(x, y)$ to $(-y, x)$: $(0, 0)$, $(0, 2)$ and $(-1, 0)$. Translating 3 right and 3 up gives $(3, 3)$, $(3, 5)$ and $(2, 3)$, which is $T'$. The other sequences give $(3, 3), (3, 1), (4, 3)$ or $(3, 3), (1, 3), (3, 4)$ or $(3, 3), (5, 3), (3, 2)$. Since a sequence of rigid moves maps $T$ onto $T'$, the triangles are congruent.

solve.answer: Rotate 90 degrees counterclockwise about the origin, then translate 3 units right and 3 units up

questions.skill: Corresponding sides of congruent triangles
questions.stem: Triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$, with $A$ matching $D$, $B$ matching $E$, and $C$ matching $F$. In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 7$ cm, $BC = 9$ cm, and $AC = 11$ cm. What is the length of $EF$, in centimeters?
questions.solution: The letters match in order, so $B$ matches $E$ and $C$ matches $F$. That makes side $EF$ match side $BC$. Matching sides of congruent triangles are equal, so $EF = BC = 9$ centimeters.

solve.work: Correspondence A-D, B-E, C-F, so EF corresponds to BC = 9 cm.

questions.skill: Naming the SSS criterion
questions.stem: Two triangles have three pairs of equal sides. Which rule shows that the two triangles are congruent?
choices: SAS
ASA
SSS
AAA
questions.answer: SSS
questions.solution: Three pairs of equal sides is the side-side-side (SSS) rule. SAS and ASA each need an angle, and equal angles alone (AAA) do not prove congruence.

solve.answer: SSS
solve.work: Three pairs of equal sides is the Side-Side-Side criterion.

questions.skill: Rigid motions and congruence
questions.stem: Which of these transformations does NOT always produce a figure congruent to the original?
choices: a dilation with scale factor 2
a translation
a reflection
a rotation
questions.answer: a dilation with scale factor 2
questions.solution: Translations, reflections and rotations are rigid motions: they keep every length and angle, so the image is congruent to the original. A dilation with scale factor 2 doubles every length, so the image is larger and not congruent.

solve.answer: a dilation with scale factor 2
solve.work: Translations, rotations and reflections are rigid motions and preserve size; a dilation with scale factor 2 doubles lengths, so the image is not congruent.

questions.skill: Recognizing the SAS criterion
questions.stem: In triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, $AB = DE = 6$, $BC = EF = 8$, and $\angle B = \angle E = 35^\circ$. Which rule shows that the triangles are congruent?
choices: ASA
SSS
AAS
SAS
questions.answer: SAS
questions.solution: $AB$ and $BC$ are the two sides that meet at $B$, so $\angle B$ lies between them. Two pairs of equal sides and the equal angle between them is the SAS rule.

solve.answer: SAS
solve.work: AB = DE, BC = EF, and angle B (between AB and BC) = angle E (between DE and EF): two sides and the included angle, SAS.

questions.skill: Using congruence to find an unknown side
questions.stem: Triangle $ABC$ is congruent to triangle $DEF$, with $A$ matching $D$, $B$ matching $E$, and $C$ matching $F$. Side $AB$ has length $2x + 1$ and side $DE$ has length $13$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: Matching sides of congruent triangles are equal, so $AB = DE$ and $2x + 1 = 13$. Subtract 1: $2x = 12$. Divide by 2: $x = 6$.

solve.work: AB corresponds to DE, so 2x + 1 = 13, 2x = 12, x = 6.

questions.skill: Why equal angles alone do not prove congruence
questions.stem: In triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, $\angle A = \angle D$, $\angle B = \angle E$, and $\angle C = \angle F$. No side lengths are known. Which statement is correct?
choices: The triangles must be congruent, because all three angles match
The triangles might not be congruent, because one could be larger than the other
The triangles cannot be congruent, because no sides are known
The triangles must be congruent by SAS
questions.answer: The triangles might not be congruent, because one could be larger than the other
questions.solution: Matching angles fix the shape of a triangle but not its size. A small triangle and an enlarged copy of it have equal angles and are not congruent, so equal angles (AAA) do not guarantee congruence.

solve.answer: The triangles might not be congruent, because one could be larger than the other
solve.work: AAA only gives similarity; one triangle can be a scaled copy of the other, so they might not be congruent. They are not impossible to be congruent (option 1 wrong), SAS needs sides (option 3 wrong), AAA is not a congruence rule (option 4 wrong).

questions.skill: The ambiguous side-side-angle case
questions.stem: In triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, $AB = DE = 8$, $BC = EF = 6$, and $\angle A = \angle D = 30^\circ$. Which statement is correct?
choices: The triangles are congruent by SAS
Congruence is not guaranteed, because the angle is not between the two known sides
The triangles are congruent by SSS
The triangles are congruent by ASA
questions.answer: Congruence is not guaranteed, because the angle is not between the two known sides
questions.solution: $\angle A$ is not the angle between sides $AB$ and $BC$; it is opposite $BC$. Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do not guarantee congruence. Here, side $BC = 6$ can swing to meet the third side in two different places, giving two different triangles.

solve.answer: Congruence is not guaranteed, because the angle is not between the two known sides
solve.work: Angle A lies between AB and AC, not between AB and BC, so this is SSA. Check ambiguity: side opposite A is BC = 6, adjacent AB = 8, height 8 sin 30 = 4; 4 < 6 < 8 so two different triangles exist. Congruence not guaranteed.

questions.skill: Proving congruence, then using it to solve
questions.stem: In triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$, $AB = DE$, $AC = DF$, and $\angle A = \angle D$. Also $BC = 4x - 3$ and $EF = 2x + 11$. What is the value of $x$?
questions.solution: $AB = DE$, $AC = DF$, and the angle between them is equal ($\angle A = \angle D$), so the triangles are congruent by SAS. Matching sides of congruent triangles are equal, so $BC = EF$: $4x - 3 = 2x + 11$. Subtract $2x$ and add 3: $2x = 14$, so $x = 7$.

solve.work: AB = DE, AC = DF, angle A = angle D is included between AB and AC, so SAS: triangles congruent, BC = EF. 4x - 3 = 2x + 11, 2x = 14, x = 7 (BC = EF = 25).

questions.skill: Arguing ASA after finding a third angle
questions.stem: Triangle $ABC$ has $\angle A = 50^\circ$, $\angle B = 60^\circ$, and $AB = 8$. Triangle $DEF$ has $\angle D = 50^\circ$, $\angle F = 70^\circ$, and $DE = 8$. Which argument is correct?
choices: Not congruent, because the $70^\circ$ angle is given for only one of the triangles
Not congruent, because only one pair of sides is known
Congruent by SAS, because $AB = DE$ and $\angle A = \angle D$
Congruent by ASA, because $\angle E = 60^\circ$ and $DE$ lies between $\angle D$ and $\angle E$
questions.answer: Congruent by ASA, because $\angle E = 60^\circ$ and $DE$ lies between $\angle D$ and $\angle E$
questions.solution: The angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$, so $\angle E = 180^\circ - 50^\circ - 70^\circ = 60^\circ$. Then $\angle A = \angle D = 50^\circ$, $\angle B = \angle E = 60^\circ$, and the side $AB = DE = 8$ lies between those two angles in each triangle. That is the ASA rule. SAS would need two pairs of equal sides.

solve.answer: Congruent by ASA, because $\angle E = 60^\circ$ and $DE$ lies between $\angle D$ and $\angle E$
solve.work: In DEF, angle E = 180 - 50 - 70 = 60. So angle A = angle D = 50, AB = DE = 8, angle B = angle E = 60; AB and DE are the included sides. ASA holds. Option 2 lacks a second side; options 3 and 4 are false.

questions.skill: Midpoint of a segment
questions.stem: What is the $x$-coordinate of the midpoint of the segment with endpoints $(2, 4)$ and $(10, 8)$?
questions.solution: The midpoint's $x$-coordinate is the average of the endpoints' $x$-coordinates: $(2 + 10) \div 2 = 6$.

solve.work: x-midpoint = (2 + 10)/2 = 6.

questions.skill: Slope of a parallel line
questions.stem: A line has slope $\frac{3}{2}$. What is the slope of any line parallel to it?
questions.solution: Parallel lines have the same slope, so a line parallel to one with slope $\frac{3}{2}$ also has slope $\frac{3}{2}$.

solve.work: Parallel lines have equal slopes: 3/2.

questions.skill: Perimeter of a rectangle from coordinates
questions.stem: A rectangle has vertices $(1, 1)$, $(7, 1)$, $(7, 4)$ and $(1, 4)$. What is its perimeter, in units?
questions.solution: The rectangle is 6 units wide (from $x = 1$ to $x = 7$) and 3 units tall (from $y = 1$ to $y = 4$). Perimeter $= 2(6) + 2(3) = 18$ units.

solve.work: Length 7 - 1 = 6, width 4 - 1 = 3. Perimeter = 2(6 + 3) = 18.

questions.skill: Slope of a perpendicular line
questions.stem: Line $l$ passes through the points $(1, 2)$ and $(5, 10)$. What is the slope of a line perpendicular to $l$?
questions.solution: The slope of $l$ is $\frac{10 - 2}{5 - 1} = \frac{8}{4} = 2$. A perpendicular line has the negative reciprocal slope: $-\frac{1}{2}$.

solve.work: Slope of l = (10 - 2)/(5 - 1) = 8/4 = 2. Perpendicular slope = -1/2.

questions.skill: Finding an endpoint from the midpoint
questions.stem: The midpoint of segment $AB$ is $(3, 5)$. Point $A$ is $(1, 2)$. What is the $y$-coordinate of point $B$?
questions.solution: The midpoint's $y$-coordinate is the average of the endpoints': $\frac{2 + y_B}{2} = 5$. So $2 + y_B = 10$ and $y_B = 8$.

questions.skill: Classifying a triangle from its vertices
questions.stem: Triangle $PQR$ has vertices $P(0, 0)$, $Q(6, 0)$ and $R(3, 4)$. What type of triangle is it?
choices: scalene
right
isosceles
equilateral
questions.answer: isosceles
questions.solution: $PQ = 6$. $PR = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$ and $QR = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$. Two sides are equal and the third is different, so the triangle is isosceles. It is not a right triangle, because $5^2 + 5^2 = 50$ is not $6^2 = 36$.

solve.answer: isosceles
solve.work: PQ = 6; PR = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5; QR = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5. Two equal sides: isosceles. Not equilateral. Right? Largest side 6: 25 + 25 = 50, not 36, so not right; other angles also not right (36 + 25 is not 25). Isosceles only.

questions.skill: Equation of a perpendicular line
questions.stem: Which is the equation of the line through $(4, 1)$ that is perpendicular to $y = 2x + 3$?
questions.solution: The slope of $y = 2x + 3$ is 2, so a perpendicular line has slope $-\frac{1}{2}$. Write $y = -\frac{1}{2}x + b$ and use the point $(4, 1)$: $1 = -2 + b$, so $b = 3$. The line $y = 2x - 7$ is parallel to the given line, not perpendicular.

solve.work: Perpendicular slope = -1/2. y - 1 = -1/2 (x - 4), y = -x/2 + 2 + 1 = -x/2 + 3. Option y = -2x + 9 passes through (4,1) but has slope -2, not perpendicular.

questions.skill: Classifying a quadrilateral from its vertices
questions.stem: Quadrilateral $ABCD$ has vertices $A(0, 0)$, $B(4, 0)$, $C(5, 3)$ and $D(1, 3)$. Which statement is true?
choices: $ABCD$ is a rectangle
$ABCD$ is a parallelogram but not a rectangle
$ABCD$ is a rhombus
$ABCD$ is not a parallelogram
questions.answer: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram but not a rectangle
questions.solution: $AB$ and $DC$ are both horizontal and 4 units long. $BC$ and $AD$ each run 1 unit across while rising 3, so they are parallel and equal in length. Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram. $AB = 4$ but $BC = \sqrt{10}$, so it is not a rhombus, and $AB$ (horizontal) is not perpendicular to $BC$ (slope 3), so it is not a rectangle.

solve.answer: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram but not a rectangle
solve.work: AB = (4,0), DC = (4,0); AD = (1,3), BC = (1,3): both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal, so a parallelogram. AB dot AD = 4, not 0, so no right angle: not a rectangle. |AB| = 4, |AD| = sqrt 10: not a rhombus.

questions.skill: Area of a triangle from coordinates
questions.stem: A triangle has vertices $(2, 1)$, $(8, 1)$ and $(11, 5)$. What is its area, in square units?
questions.solution: The side from $(2, 1)$ to $(8, 1)$ is horizontal and 6 units long; use it as the base. The height is the vertical distance from the line $y = 1$ to the point $(11, 5)$, which is 4. Area $= \frac{1}{2}(6)(4) = 12$ square units.

solve.work: Base from (2,1) to (8,1) has length 6 on the line y = 1. Height = 5 - 1 = 4. Area = 1/2 x 6 x 4 = 12. (Shoelace check: 2(1-5) + 8(5-1) + 11(1-1) = -8 + 32 = 24, half = 12.)

questions.skill: Marginal total from a two-way table
questions.stem: A survey asked 40 students how they get to school. Of the 24 boys, 15 walk. Of the 16 girls, 7 walk. How many of the 40 students walk?
questions.solution: Add the boys who walk and the girls who walk: $15 + 7 = 22$.

solve.work: Walkers = 15 boys + 7 girls = 22.

questions.skill: Probability of a complement
questions.stem: In a class of 30 students, 12 have a pet. One student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student does NOT have a pet?
questions.solution: Students without a pet: $30 - 12 = 18$. The probability is $\frac{18}{30} = \frac{3}{5}$. The fraction $\frac{2}{5}$ is the probability of having a pet.

questions.skill: Joint probability from a two-way table
questions.stem: In a survey of 50 students, 14 are in grade 9 and play an instrument, 10 are in grade 9 and do not, 16 are in grade 10 and play an instrument, and 10 are in grade 10 and do not. One of the 50 students is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student is in grade 9 and plays an instrument? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: 14 of the 50 students are both in grade 9 and play an instrument, so the probability is $\frac{14}{50} = \frac{7}{25}$.

solve.work: Check total 14 + 10 + 16 + 10 = 50. P(grade 9 and plays) = 14/50 = 7/25.

questions.skill: Finding a missing entry in a two-way table
questions.stem: A survey of 80 students recorded each student's favorite pet. Every student chose cats or dogs. Of the students, 48 are girls. Among the girls, 30 chose cats. Among the boys, 22 chose cats. How many boys chose dogs?
questions.solution: Boys: $80 - 48 = 32$. Of these 32 boys, 22 chose cats, so $32 - 22 = 10$ chose dogs. (The 30 girls who chose cats are not needed.)

solve.work: Boys = 80 - 48 = 32. Boys choosing cats = 22, so boys choosing dogs = 32 - 22 = 10.

questions.skill: Probability of a union
questions.stem: In a group of 40 students, 18 take Spanish, 15 take French, and 6 take both. One student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student takes Spanish or French (or both)?
questions.solution: Adding 18 and 15 counts the 6 students who take both twice, so subtract them once: $18 + 15 - 6 = 27$. The probability is $\frac{27}{40}$.

solve.work: Spanish or French = 18 + 15 - 6 = 27. P = 27/40.

questions.skill: Marginal probability from a two-way table
questions.stem: A cafe recorded 50 orders: 12 adults ordered coffee, 8 teens ordered coffee, 20 adults ordered tea, and 10 teens ordered tea. One order is chosen at random. What is the probability that it was ordered by a teen?
questions.solution: Teens ordered $8 + 10 = 18$ of the 50 orders, so the probability is $\frac{18}{50} = \frac{9}{25}$. The fraction $\frac{1}{5}$ is only the teens who ordered tea.

questions.skill: Intersection from a union and a complement
questions.stem: Of 50 students, 30 play soccer, 25 play basketball, and 8 play neither sport. How many students play both?
questions.solution: The students who play at least one sport number $50 - 8 = 42$. Adding the soccer and basketball players gives $30 + 25 = 55$, which counts the students who play both twice. So the number who play both is $55 - 42 = 13$.

solve.work: At least one sport = 50 - 8 = 42. Both = 30 + 25 - 42 = 13. (Soccer only 17, basketball only 12, both 13, neither 8: total 50.)

questions.skill: Using a two-way table with several given totals
questions.stem: Of 100 students, 60 are in grade 9 and the rest are in grade 10. In all, 45 of the students ride the bus, and 28 of the grade 9 students ride the bus. One student is chosen at random. What is the probability that the student is in grade 10 and does not ride the bus? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Grade 10 students: $100 - 60 = 40$. Grade 10 students who ride the bus: $45 - 28 = 17$. Grade 10 students who do not ride the bus: $40 - 17 = 23$. The probability is $\frac{23}{100}$.

solve.work: Grade 10 = 100 - 60 = 40. Grade 10 bus riders = 45 - 28 = 17. Grade 10 not on bus = 40 - 17 = 23. P = 23/100.

questions.skill: Probability from a sample space
questions.stem: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is NOT 8? Write your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: There are $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely outcomes. The sum is 8 for $(2,6)$, $(3,5)$, $(4,4)$, $(5,3)$ and $(6,2)$: 5 outcomes. So $P(\text{sum is } 8) = \frac{5}{36}$ and $P(\text{not } 8) = 1 - \frac{5}{36} = \frac{31}{36}$.

questions.skill: Telling a statistical question from a non-statistical one
questions.stem: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: How many hours do students at our school sleep on school nights?
How tall is the tallest tree in the park?
What is the sum of 14 and 9?
How many students are in Ms. Lee's class today?
questions.answer: How many hours do students at our school sleep on school nights?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects the answers to vary. Students sleep different numbers of hours, so the data will vary. The other three questions each have one fixed answer.

solve.answer: How many hours do students at our school sleep on school nights?
solve.work: A statistical question anticipates variability in the data. Sleep hours of students vary from student to student. The others each have one fixed answer (a sum, one tallest tree, one class count).

questions.skill: Categorical and numerical variables
questions.stem: For each student in a survey, a researcher records favorite color, number of siblings, height in centimeters, and minutes taken to run a mile. Which of these variables is categorical?
choices: number of siblings
height in centimeters
minutes taken to run a mile
favorite color
questions.answer: favorite color
questions.solution: A categorical variable puts each person into a group or category, such as a color. The other three are measured or counted as numbers.

solve.answer: favorite color
solve.work: Favorite color is a category; minutes, siblings and height are numerical.

questions.skill: Sampling bias from convenience
questions.stem: Maya wants to know the favorite lunch of all the students at her school, so she asks only the students at her own lunch table. Why might her results be biased?
choices: She asked about lunch, and lunch choices cannot be counted
Her table may not represent all of the students at the school
She asked too many students
She did not ask any teachers
questions.answer: Her table may not represent all of the students at the school
questions.solution: Her friends at one table may have different tastes from the rest of the school, so the sample may not represent all students. That is a biased sample.

solve.answer: Her table may not represent all of the students at the school
solve.work: A convenience sample of one lunch table may not represent the whole school.

questions.skill: Counting statistical questions
questions.stem: Here are five questions. (A) How tall is the flagpole at our school? (B) How tall are the students at our school? (C) How many sides does a hexagon have? (D) How fast do drivers travel on Oak Street? (E) What is today's date? How many of the five are statistical questions?
questions.solution: A statistical question expects varying answers. (B) and (D) do: students differ in height and drivers differ in speed. (A), (C) and (E) each have one fixed answer. So 2 are statistical.

solve.work: (A) one flagpole, one height: not statistical. (B) heights vary among students: statistical. (C) six: not. (D) speeds vary among drivers: statistical. (E) one date: not. Count = 2.

questions.skill: Voluntary response bias
questions.stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in to vote on whether the town needs a new park. It then reports the result as the opinion of the whole town. What is the main problem?
choices: So many people called that the data cannot be organized
Only listeners who choose to call are counted, so the votes may not represent the whole town
The question has more than one possible answer
Radio stations are not allowed to collect data
questions.answer: Only listeners who choose to call are counted, so the votes may not represent the whole town
questions.solution: Only people who listen and care enough to call are included (voluntary response), so they may differ from the town as a whole.

solve.answer: Only listeners who choose to call are counted, so the votes may not represent the whole town
solve.work: Voluntary-response sample: only listeners who choose to call are counted, so it may not represent the town.

questions.skill: Explain how non-response biases a survey
questions.stem: A survey about school lunches was sent to 400 randomly chosen students. Only 100 of them sent it back, mostly students with strong opinions about the lunches. Why might the results be biased?
choices: Choosing students at random always gives biased results
The students who replied may differ from those who did not
Surveying 400 students is too many to be fair
The students should all have been in the same grade
questions.answer: The students who replied may differ from those who did not
questions.solution: The students were chosen at random, which is a good way to sample. But three quarters of them did not reply, and the ones who did mostly have strong opinions. Their answers may not match the views of the students who stayed silent, so the results may be biased. A large sample and a mix of grades do not cause bias.

solve.answer: The students who replied may differ from those who did not
solve.work: Only 100 of 400 replied, mostly those with strong opinions: voluntary response / nonresponse bias. The responders may not represent those who did not reply. Random selection does not always bias; same grade is irrelevant; 400 is not 'too many'.

questions.skill: Biased survey wording
questions.stem: Which survey question about the school cafeteria is the most neutral (least biased)?
choices: Don't you agree that the cafeteria food is terrible and should be changed?
Most students love the new menu. Do you love it too?
Wouldn't you say the cafeteria needs more healthy options?
How would you rate the cafeteria food: poor, fair, good, or excellent?
questions.answer: How would you rate the cafeteria food: poor, fair, good, or excellent?
questions.solution: The other three questions push the reader toward a particular answer (leading questions). The rating question offers balanced choices and does not suggest which to pick.

solve.answer: How would you rate the cafeteria food: poor, fair, good, or excellent?
solve.work: The rating scale question does not suggest an answer. The others are leading (love it too, don't you agree it is terrible, wouldn't you say it needs more).

questions.skill: Choosing an unbiased sampling method
questions.stem: A school has 1,200 students. Which method is most likely to give an unbiased estimate of the average time students spend on homework?
choices: Ask 100 students chosen at random from the full list of students
Ask all 30 members of the math club
Ask the first 50 students who arrive at school in the morning
Ask the 100 students who are in the library after school
questions.answer: Ask 100 students chosen at random from the full list of students
questions.solution: A random sample from the complete list gives every student an equal chance of being chosen. The other groups are likely to spend more or less time on homework than the typical student.

solve.answer: Ask 100 students chosen at random from the full list of students
solve.work: A simple random sample from the full list is unbiased; early arrivals, library students and math club are convenience groups likely to differ in homework time.

questions.skill: Questions a dataset can answer
questions.stem: A student collects data from her classmates on three things: hours of sleep, hours of screen time, and last test score. Which question can she investigate with this data?
choices: Which classmates prefer pizza to pasta?
How many hours do students in other countries sleep?
Is there a relationship between hours of sleep and test score among her classmates?
Will the school's fire alarm be replaced next year?
questions.answer: Is there a relationship between hours of sleep and test score among her classmates?
questions.solution: A question can be investigated only with data that has been collected. Sleep and test score were recorded for each classmate, so she can look for a relationship between them. The other questions need data she does not have.

solve.answer: Is there a relationship between hours of sleep and test score among her classmates?
solve.work: She has sleep, screen time and test score for her classmates, so she can study a relationship between sleep and test score among them. The others need data she did not collect.

questions.skill: Judging the credibility of a source
questions.stem: Which source is the most credible for finding the average number of students per class in a state's public schools?
choices: A social media post by an anonymous account that gives no sources
An advertisement from a company that sells school supplies
A classmate's estimate based on only her own class
A report from the state education agency that explains how its data were collected
questions.answer: A report from the state education agency that explains how its data were collected
questions.solution: A credible source is open about how its data were collected and covers the whole group. The other sources give no method, may have a reason to exaggerate, or look at only one class.

solve.answer: A report from the state education agency that explains how its data were collected
solve.work: An official agency report that documents its methods is the most credible; the others are anonymous, anecdotal or commercially motivated.

questions.skill: Choosing relevant variables
questions.stem: A student wants to predict the selling price of a house. Which variable is the LEAST useful for this?
choices: the size of the house in square feet
the favorite color of the owner
the number of bedrooms
the neighborhood
questions.answer: the favorite color of the owner
questions.solution: Size, number of bedrooms and neighborhood all affect what buyers pay. The owner's favorite color has no connection to the price.

solve.answer: the favorite color of the owner
solve.work: Size, bedrooms and neighborhood all relate to price; the owner's favorite color does not.

questions.skill: Choose the variables that answer a question
questions.stem: Sara wants to know whether students who sleep more tend to score higher on quizzes. For each classmate she records hours of sleep, quiz score, shoe size and favorite color. Which two variables should she compare?
choices: Shoe size and favorite color
Hours of sleep and shoe size
Hours of sleep and quiz score
Quiz score and favorite color
questions.answer: Hours of sleep and quiz score
questions.solution: Her question is about sleep and quiz scores, so those are the two variables that matter. Shoe size and favorite color have nothing to do with her question, so pairs that include them would not help her answer it.

solve.answer: Hours of sleep and quiz score
solve.work: The question is whether more sleep goes with higher quiz scores, so the relevant variables are hours of sleep (explanatory) and quiz score (response). Shoe size and favorite color are irrelevant.

questions.skill: Recognizing a third variable
questions.stem: A dataset shows that students who own more books tend to have higher reading scores. A researcher thinks a student's age may affect both the number of books and the reading score. In this situation, how is age best described?
choices: The only cause of the higher reading scores
A variable that can be ignored because it was not in the question
A third variable that may influence both of the others
A sign that the data were collected incorrectly
questions.answer: A third variable that may influence both of the others
questions.solution: Older students may own more books and also read better. Age is then a third variable related to both, and it can help explain the pattern. It should not be ignored, and it does not mean the data are wrong.

solve.answer: A third variable that may influence both of the others
solve.work: Age may influence both books owned and reading score: a third (lurking/confounding) variable.

questions.skill: Comparing two groups
questions.stem: Of 50 students who used a study app, 35 passed the test. Of 50 students who did not use the app, 30 passed. How many percentage points higher is the pass percent of the app group than the pass percent of the other group?
questions.solution: App group: $\frac{35}{50} = 70$ percent. Other group: $\frac{30}{50} = 60$ percent. The difference is $70 - 60 = 10$ percentage points.

solve.work: App group 35/50 = 70 percent; other group 30/50 = 60 percent. Difference = 10 percentage points.

questions.skill: Doubting a claim about data
questions.stem: A website says, "Our vitamin drink raises math scores by 30 percent!" Which detail would make you the MOST doubtful of the claim?
choices: The website sells the drink and does not say how scores were measured
The study included a comparison group that did not drink it
The study reports how many students took part
The data were collected by an outside research team
questions.answer: The website sells the drink and does not say how scores were measured
questions.solution: A seller with something to gain, and no information on how the scores were measured, is a reason to doubt. A comparison group, a stated number of students and independent researchers all make a claim more credible.

solve.answer: The website sells the drink and does not say how scores were measured
solve.work: A seller with an interest in the result who gives no measurement method is the most reason for doubt; the other details make the claim more credible.

questions.skill: Splitting data by a third variable
questions.stem: Two tutoring programs report results. Program X had 80 beginners, 48 of whom passed, and 20 advanced students, 19 of whom passed. Program Y had 20 beginners, 10 of whom passed, and 80 advanced students, 70 of whom passed. Program X has the higher pass rate at each level, yet Program Y has the higher pass rate overall. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Program Y must have recorded its results incorrectly
Program X is actually worse than Program Y at every level
Program X had a much larger share of beginners, who pass less often in both programs
Percentages from small groups should always be ignored
questions.answer: Program X had a much larger share of beginners, who pass less often in both programs
questions.solution: Beginners: X passed $\frac{48}{80} = 60$ percent, Y passed $\frac{10}{20} = 50$ percent. Advanced: X passed $\frac{19}{20} = 95$ percent, Y passed $\frac{70}{80} = 87.5$ percent. So X is higher at both levels. Overall, X passed $\frac{67}{100}$ and Y passed $\frac{80}{100}$. Most of X's students were beginners, who pass less often in either program, which pulls X's overall rate down.

solve.answer: Program X had a much larger share of beginners, who pass less often in both programs
solve.work: X: beginners 48/80 = 60, advanced 19/20 = 95, overall 67/100 = 67 percent. Y: beginners 10/20 = 50, advanced 70/80 = 87.5, overall 80/100 = 80 percent. X wins in each level, Y overall (Simpson's paradox) because X has 80 percent beginners, who pass less often in both programs.

questions.skill: Combining group means
questions.stem: In a dataset, 20 students in group A have a mean quiz score of 70, and 30 students in group B have a mean quiz score of 90. What is the mean quiz score of all 50 students?
questions.solution: Total points in group A: $20 \times 70 = 1{,}400$. Total points in group B: $30 \times 90 = 2{,}700$. All 50 students: $\frac{1{,}400 + 2{,}700}{50} = \frac{4{,}100}{50} = 82$.

questions.skill: Splitting data to improve a model
questions.stem: A student plots test score against hours studied for 60 students and finds only a weak pattern. She then separates the students into a morning class and an evening class. Each group shows a clear, steady pattern, but the two patterns are different. What does this suggest?
choices: Class time is a third variable that should be included in the analysis
Hours studied has no relationship with test score
The data should be thrown away because the first pattern was weak
Evening students are better at math than morning students
questions.answer: Class time is a third variable that should be included in the analysis
questions.solution: The weak overall pattern comes from mixing two groups with different patterns. Splitting by class time reveals the relationship in each group, so class time should be part of the model.

solve.answer: Class time is a third variable that should be included in the analysis
solve.work: Splitting by class reveals clear but different patterns, so class time is a third variable that should be included. Hours studied clearly does relate within groups, so option 1 is wrong; option 4 is not supported.

questions.skill: Describing direction and form
questions.stem: A scatter plot has the points $(1, 2)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 5)$, $(4, 7)$ and $(5, 9)$. Which best describes the pattern?
choices: negative and roughly linear
no clear pattern
a curve that levels off
positive and roughly linear
questions.answer: positive and roughly linear
questions.solution: As $x$ increases, $y$ increases steadily by about 2 each time, so the points rise along a roughly straight line: a positive, roughly linear association.

solve.answer: positive and roughly linear
solve.work: y increases with x by 2,1,2,2: positive and close to a straight line.

questions.skill: Reading a point on a scatter plot
questions.stem: In a scatter plot, each point is (hours studied, quiz score). What does the point $(3, 78)$ mean?
choices: A student studied for 78 hours and scored 3
A student studied for 3 hours and scored 78
Three students each scored 78
A student scored 3 points higher after studying for 78 hours
questions.answer: A student studied for 3 hours and scored 78
questions.solution: The first number is the hours studied and the second is the quiz score, so the point is a student who studied 3 hours and scored 78.

solve.answer: A student studied for 3 hours and scored 78
solve.work: x = hours studied = 3, y = quiz score = 78: a student studied 3 hours and scored 78.

questions.skill: Predicting from a line of best fit
questions.stem: A line of best fit for hours studied ($x$) and quiz score ($y$) is $y = 4x + 50$. Use the line to predict the quiz score of a student who studies 6 hours.

questions.skill: Comparing the strength of associations
choices: Q shows a stronger linear association than P
P shows a stronger linear association than Q
P and Q show equally strong associations, because both go upward
Q shows a negative association and P a positive one
questions.answer: P shows a stronger linear association than Q
questions.solution: Every point of P lies exactly on the line $y = 2x$, a perfectly strong linear association. Q rises overall but its points are scattered above and below any line, so the association is positive and weaker.

solve.answer: P shows a stronger linear association than Q
solve.work: P lies exactly on y = 2x (perfect linear). Q rises overall (3,2,6,5,8) but zigzags, so its linear association is weaker. Both positive.

questions.skill: Slope of a line of best fit
questions.stem: A line of best fit for the age of a car, $x$ (in years), and its value, $y$ (in thousands of dollars), passes through $(2, 18)$ and $(6, 10)$. What is the slope of the line?
questions.solution: Slope $= \frac{10 - 18}{6 - 2} = \frac{-8}{4} = -2$. The value drops by 2 thousand dollars for each extra year of age.

questions.skill: Recognizing a nonlinear form
questions.stem: A scatter plot has the points $(0, 1)$, $(1, 2)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 8)$ and $(4, 16)$. Which kind of model fits these points best?
choices: A straight line with positive slope
A straight line with negative slope
No pattern at all
A curve that rises faster and faster
questions.answer: A curve that rises faster and faster
questions.solution: The $y$-values double each time $x$ goes up by 1 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16), so the points rise by larger and larger amounts. They follow an upward curve, not a straight line.

solve.answer: A curve that rises faster and faster
solve.work: y doubles each step (1,2,4,8,16): exponential growth, a curve rising faster and faster.

questions.skill: Interpreting the slope of a line of best fit
questions.stem: A line of best fit for hours of practice ($x$) and test score ($y$) is $y = 3x + 40$. Which is the best interpretation of the slope, 3?
choices: Each extra hour of practice goes with about 3 more points, on average
A student who does not practice scores about 3
A student who practices 3 hours scores exactly 40
Each extra point goes with about 3 more hours of practice
questions.answer: Each extra hour of practice goes with about 3 more points, on average
questions.solution: The slope is the change in $y$ for each 1-unit increase in $x$: each extra hour of practice goes with about 3 more points of score, on average. The 40 is the predicted score for 0 hours.

solve.answer: Each extra hour of practice goes with about 3 more points, on average
solve.work: Slope 3 = predicted change in score per extra hour of practice: about 3 more points per hour on average.

questions.skill: Predicting from two points on a line
