questions.stem: A line of best fit passes through $(1, 12)$ and $(5, 20)$. Use the line to predict $y$ when $x = 8$.
questions.solution: Slope $= \frac{20 - 12}{5 - 1} = 2$. From $x = 1$ to $x = 8$ is 7 units, so $y$ rises by $2 \times 7 = 14$ from 12: $y = 26$.

questions.skill: Critiquing a misleading display
questions.stem: A news graph shows the test pass rates of two classes as bars. Class A's pass rate is 90 percent and Class B's is 85 percent. The vertical axis starts at 80 percent instead of 0, so Class A's bar looks twice as tall as Class B's. Why is this display misleading?
choices: Bars should never be used to compare two classes
The pass rates should have been shown as decimals
Starting the axis at 80 makes a small difference look much larger than it is
Class B's bar should be taller because its class is smaller
questions.answer: Starting the axis at 80 makes a small difference look much larger than it is
questions.solution: With the axis starting at 80, the bars show heights of 10 and 5, which looks like a 2-to-1 difference. The real pass rates, 90 and 85 percent, differ by only 5 points.

solve.answer: Starting the axis at 80 makes a small difference look much larger than it is
solve.work: Bars from 80: A shows 10, B shows 5, so A looks twice as tall although the difference is only 5 points. Truncated axis exaggerates the difference.

questions.skill: Strength of a correlation coefficient
questions.stem: Four data sets have these correlation coefficients, $r$. Which value shows the strongest linear relationship?
questions.solution: The strength of a linear relationship depends on how close $r$ is to $1$ or $-1$, not on its sign. Of the four, $-0.9$ is the closest to $-1$, so it is the strongest.

questions.skill: Computing a residual
questions.stem: A residual is the actual value minus the predicted value. A line predicts a quiz score of 47 for a student, but the student actually scored 52. What is the residual?
questions.solution: Residual $=$ actual $-$ predicted $= 52 - 47 = 5$.

solve.work: Residual = 52 - 47 = 5.

questions.skill: Correlation is not causation
questions.stem: Data show that towns with more ice cream sales also have more sunburns. What is the best conclusion?
choices: Eating ice cream causes people to get sunburned
Hot, sunny weather may cause both, so the data do not show that ice cream causes sunburns
Getting sunburned causes people to buy more ice cream
There is no relationship between ice cream sales and sunburns
questions.answer: Hot, sunny weather may cause both, so the data do not show that ice cream causes sunburns
questions.solution: The two go up together, so they are correlated. But a third variable, hot sunny weather, can explain both. A correlation alone does not show that one thing causes the other.

solve.answer: Hot, sunny weather may cause both, so the data do not show that ice cream causes sunburns
solve.work: Correlation is not causation; hot sunny weather is a likely common cause of both.

questions.skill: Predicting from a least-squares line
questions.stem: The least-squares line for a plant's height, $y$ (in centimeters), after $x$ weeks is $\hat{y} = 1.5x + 12.4$. Use the line to predict the height after 6 weeks, in centimeters.
questions.solution: Substitute $x = 6$: $\hat{y} = 1.5(6) + 12.4 = 9 + 12.4 = 21.4$ centimeters.

questions.skill: Judging an extrapolated prediction
questions.stem: A line fits the heights of children aged 5 to 12 well. A student uses the line to predict the height of a 40-year-old. Why is this prediction unreliable?
choices: Predictions from a line of best fit are never reliable
A line of best fit must pass through every point to be used
Age 40 is far outside the ages in the data, and the pattern may not continue
Height cannot be predicted from age at all
questions.answer: Age 40 is far outside the ages in the data, and the pattern may not continue
questions.solution: The line was fitted to ages 5 to 12. Predicting far outside that range (extrapolating) assumes the same pattern continues, but people stop growing as they become adults.

solve.answer: Age 40 is far outside the ages in the data, and the pattern may not continue
solve.work: Extrapolation far outside the data range (5-12); growth stops in adulthood so the line will not hold.

questions.skill: Meaning of an exponential growth factor
questions.stem: A town's population is modeled by $P = 2{,}000(1.05)^t$, where $t$ is the number of years. What does the 1.05 tell you?
choices: The population grows by 5 percent each year
The population grows by 105 percent each year
The population grows by 1.05 people each year
The population shrinks by 5 percent each year
questions.answer: The population grows by 5 percent each year
questions.solution: Each year the population is multiplied by 1.05, which is 100 percent plus 5 percent. So it grows by 5 percent each year.

solve.answer: The population grows by 5 percent each year
solve.work: Growth factor 1.05 = 1 + 0.05: the population grows by 5 percent each year (it becomes 105 percent of the previous year, not grows by 105 percent).

questions.skill: Effect of an outlier on correlation
questions.stem: For a set of 20 data points, $r = 0.45$. After one point that lies far from the pattern is removed, $r$ becomes $0.92$. What does this suggest about that point?
choices: It proved that the two variables are not related
Removing any point always raises the correlation
It was an outlier that was weakening the linear pattern
The two variables now cause each other
questions.answer: It was an outlier that was weakening the linear pattern
questions.solution: The remaining 19 points follow a strong linear pattern ($r = 0.92$). The one point far from it pulled the correlation down, so it is an outlier. Removing a point does not always raise $r$, and a correlation never proves cause.

solve.answer: It was an outlier that was weakening the linear pattern
solve.work: Removing one far-off point raised r from 0.45 to 0.92, so that point was an outlier weakening the linear pattern.

questions.skill: Evaluating an exponential model
questions.stem: The value of a car is modeled by $V = 20{,}000(0.9)^t$, where $V$ is its value in dollars and $t$ is its age in years. What is the value of the car after 2 years, in dollars?

questions.skill: Reading a residual plot
questions.stem: A residual plot for a linear model shows the residuals forming a clear U-shaped curve instead of a random scatter around 0. What does this suggest?
choices: A straight line is not the best model; a curve may fit better
The linear model fits the data perfectly
The correlation coefficient must be exactly 0
Every data point is an outlier
questions.answer: A straight line is not the best model; a curve may fit better
questions.solution: A good linear model leaves residuals scattered randomly around 0. A clear curved pattern in the residuals means the data bend away from a straight line, so a curved model, such as an exponential one, may fit better.

solve.answer: A straight line is not the best model; a curve may fit better
solve.work: A curved pattern in residuals means the linear model misses curvature; a nonlinear model may fit better.

questions.skill: Reporting a conclusion accurately
questions.stem: In a random sample of 100 students, 60 said they prefer online homework. Which statement reports this accurately?
choices: 60 percent of all students everywhere prefer online homework
Online homework is better for learning
Exactly 60 percent of the students in the school prefer online homework
In the sample, 60 percent of the students prefer online homework
questions.answer: In the sample, 60 percent of the students prefer online homework
questions.solution: The data tell us what happened in the sample: 60 of 100 students prefer online homework. They do not show that online homework is better for learning, and a sample cannot tell us the exact percent for everyone.

solve.answer: In the sample, 60 percent of the students prefer online homework
solve.work: 60/100 = 60 percent of the sample. The other options over-generalize, claim exactness for the school, or claim causation.

questions.skill: Steps of a statistical investigation
questions.stem: A class carries out a statistical investigation. Which step should come first?
choices: Collect the data
Pose a statistical question
Analyze the data
Share the conclusions
questions.answer: Pose a statistical question
questions.solution: An investigation starts by asking a question that data can answer. Then the data are collected, analyzed, and the conclusions are shared.

solve.answer: Pose a statistical question
solve.work: The investigation process begins with posing a statistical question, then collecting, analyzing, interpreting/sharing.

questions.skill: Judge whether a claim in an ad can be trusted
questions.stem: An ad says, "9 out of 10 people we asked like our juice best." Which information would help you decide whether the claim can be trusted?
choices: What color the juice bottle is
How many seconds long the ad is
How many people were asked, and how they were picked
How much one bottle of juice costs
questions.answer: How many people were asked, and how they were picked
questions.solution: To trust "9 out of 10", you need to know about the survey itself: how many people were asked and how they were chosen. If only 10 friends of the company were asked, the claim says little. The color of the bottle, the length of the ad and the price do not tell you whether the survey was fair.

solve.answer: How many people were asked, and how they were picked
solve.work: Trusting a survey claim depends on the sample size and how the sample was chosen (e.g., only asking existing customers). Bottle color, price and ad length say nothing about the claim's reliability.

questions.skill: Limits of conclusions from an observational study
questions.stem: A study at one school finds that students who exercise more have higher grades. Which conclusion is best supported by the study?
choices: Exercise causes higher grades for all students in the country
Exercise and grades are associated here, but this does not show that exercise causes higher grades
Higher grades cause students to exercise more
Exercise has no effect on grades
questions.answer: Exercise and grades are associated here, but this does not show that exercise causes higher grades
questions.solution: The study found an association at one school. It does not show cause and effect in either direction, and it cannot speak for all students in the country.

solve.answer: Exercise and grades are associated here, but this does not show that exercise causes higher grades
solve.work: An observational study at one school shows association only, not causation, and cannot be generalized to the country.

questions.skill: Critiquing a percent-change claim
questions.stem: An ad says, "Our tutoring raised average quiz scores by 50 percent!" The average score went from 2 points to 3 points out of 100. Why is the claim misleading?
choices: A 50 percent increase is not possible with quiz scores
The score should have gone from 2 to 4 for a 50 percent increase
Percentages should never be used in advertising
A small starting value makes a gain of 1 point look like a large percent increase
questions.answer: A small starting value makes a gain of 1 point look like a large percent increase
questions.solution: Going from 2 to 3 is an increase of 1 point, which is $\frac{1}{2} = 50$ percent of the starting score, so the 50 percent is correct. But both scores are tiny out of 100, so the percent makes a very small gain sound large.

solve.answer: A small starting value makes a gain of 1 point look like a large percent increase
solve.work: 2 to 3 is indeed a 50 percent increase (1/2), but it is only 1 point out of 100; the small base makes the gain look large. Option 1 is false (2 to 4 is 100 percent).

questions.skill: Applying a sample result to a population
questions.stem: A report says that 18 of the 24 students in a sample improved. Suppose the same percent of all 600 students in the school improved. How many students would that be?
questions.solution: $\frac{18}{24} = 0.75$, which is 75 percent. 75 percent of 600 is $0.75 \times 600 = 450$ students.

questions.skill: Generalizing beyond the sample
questions.stem: A student surveys 30 classmates in her homeroom about screen time. She then states, "Students in our whole district spend about 3 hours a day on screens." Which is the best critique?
choices: Her homeroom was not a random sample of the district, so the claim may not apply to all students
She should have surveyed fewer students
Screen time cannot be measured in hours
She should have surveyed only students who use screens a lot
questions.answer: Her homeroom was not a random sample of the district, so the claim may not apply to all students
questions.solution: One homeroom is not chosen at random from the district, so it may differ from the other students. A conclusion about the whole district needs a sample that represents the district.

solve.answer: Her homeroom was not a random sample of the district, so the claim may not apply to all students
solve.work: One homeroom is a convenience sample, not random or representative of the district, so generalizing to the district is not justified.

questions.skill: Critiquing an average in the media
questions.stem: A news report says, "The average (mean) home price in the town is 450 thousand dollars." Most homes sold for about 200 thousand dollars, but a few very large homes sold for over 2 million dollars. Which is the best critique?
choices: The mean is always the best measure of a typical value
The report should have used the largest price instead
A few very expensive homes raise the mean, so the median would describe a typical home better
The report is correct because most homes cost 450 thousand dollars
questions.answer: A few very expensive homes raise the mean, so the median would describe a typical home better
questions.solution: The very expensive homes pull the mean far above what most homes cost. The median is not affected much by a few extreme values, so it describes a typical home better here.

solve.answer: A few very expensive homes raise the mean, so the median would describe a typical home better
solve.work: Right-skewed prices: a few very expensive homes pull the mean far above the typical 200 thousand; the median is a better measure of a typical home.

questions.skill: What a report should include
questions.stem: A student finishes a statistical investigation and writes a report for her class. Which should the report include so that readers can judge the conclusions fairly?
choices: Only the results that support her conclusion
Only the final conclusion, without how the data were collected
Her opinion of which classmates answered best
How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and what the data cannot show
questions.answer: How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and what the data cannot show
questions.solution: Readers need to know how the data were gathered and what the study can and cannot tell them. Leaving out opposing results or the method hides information they need.

solve.answer: How the sample was chosen, how many were included, and what the data cannot show
solve.work: A fair report states the sampling method, sample size and limitations; the other options hide information or add bias.
